sections.heading: Wholesale colocation: the operator-landlord model
bullets: Retail colocation rents racks and cages to many small customers with cross-connect fees; wholesale colocation leases whole data halls, buildings or campuses to a handful of giant tenants under multi-year contracts — fewer, bigger, stickier deals
The wholesale operator-landlord owns the land, building, power infrastructure and cooling plant, and operates them 24/7; the tenant installs and owns the IT gear (servers, GPUs, networking)
Leases are typically take-or-pay: rent is owed on the reserved megawatts whether or not the tenant fills them — which is what makes the cash flows financeable like infrastructure, not like tech
Build-to-suit goes one step further: the campus is designed around one named tenant's requirements before ground breaks, trading spec-build risk for a locked anchor

sections.heading: Powered shell vs turnkey: who supplies what
bullets: A powered shell is the building plus utility power connection only — the tenant installs its own electrical distribution, UPS, generators and cooling. Cheapest rent, longest tenant fit-out

Turnkey (full-service wholesale) delivers the complete environment — power distribution, backup, cooling, security, operations staff — so the tenant just rolls in racks. Higher rent, fastest time to compute

Vantage's model is turnkey at campus scale: it standardizes one 'sustainable by design' blueprint (closed-loop chilled water, liquid-ready cooling, common electrical topology) and replicates it across every campus
Why hyperscalers accept turnkey premiums: their scarce resource is time-to-power — a proven landlord who delivers 100MW+ buildings on schedule beats saving a few percent on rent

sections.heading: The campus development lifecycle: land and power banking to fit-out
bullets: Step 1 — land/power banking: acquire large parcels (hundreds to 1,200+ acres) where utility power can be secured; the land is cheap, the megawatts are the real asset

Step 2 — the interconnection queue: utilities and grid operators process connection requests in order, often taking 3-5 years for gigawatt loads; a secured 400MW connection (like the Bordeaux site Vantage partnered into) is worth more than the dirt under it
Step 3 — entitlement and shell: zoning, permits, tax agreements, then vertical construction of the building shell and substation — 12-24 months for a large building
Step 4 — fit-out and energization: electrical rooms, cooling plant, commissioning, then the tenant's own gear; revenue starts at 'ready for service', so schedule slip is lost rent
Developers pipeline these steps across many campuses at once — which is why 'GW of capacity' claims always mix operational, under-construction and merely-banked megawatts; read the fine print

sections.heading: Giga-campus economics and the 250kW rack
bullets: AI training clusters concentrate power: a traditional enterprise rack draws 5-15kW, modern GPU racks draw 130kW+, and next-generation designs (what Frontier is built for) exceed 250kW per rack — 1.4kW per square foot of building
Density changes the building: at 250kW/rack, air cannot carry the heat away — liquid must touch the rack, floors carry more weight, and electrical rooms grow relative to white space
Scale changes the math: a 1.4GW campus at roughly $18M+ per MW all-in (Frontier: $25B+ for 1.4GW) is a bet no one makes on spec — mega-campuses exist because a creditworthy tenant committed first

Single-story vs multi-story: cheap remote land (Shackelford County) gets 10 sprawling single-story halls; expensive metro land (Reno, London) gets multi-story buildings — same blueprint, different verticality

sections.heading: PUE, WUE and the cooling stack
bullets: PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) = total facility power ÷ IT power. A PUE of 1.5 means 50% overhead on top of every IT watt; modern hyperscale designs run 1.1-1.3. On 900MW of IT, each 0.1 of PUE is ~90MW of pure overhead

WUE (Water Usage Effectiveness) = liters of water per kWh of IT energy. Evaporative cooling saves electricity by evaporating water — cheap PUE, terrible WUE. Communities increasingly veto water-hungry designs

The closed-loop answer: chill water once, circulate it forever through air-cooled chillers — no evaporation, WUE near zero, at the cost of somewhat higher electrical overhead. This is Vantage's standard fleet design

The liquid ladder: air cooling (to ~30-40kW/rack) → rear-door heat exchangers → liquid-to-liquid CDUs (coolant distribution units) serving direct-to-chip cold plates (100kW+ racks). Vantage's VA4 is its first campus where CDUs can carry 100% of the IT load
Free cooling: when outside air is cold enough, compressors idle and PUE drops — a structural advantage for Wales, Wisconsin, Quebec and Zurich over Phoenix and Johor

sections.heading: Behind-the-meter power: microgrids and bridge generation
bullets: Behind-the-meter means generation connected on the customer's side of the utility meter — the campus makes its own power instead of (or before) drawing from the grid, sidestepping the interconnection queue entirely

Reciprocating gas engines (like the 210 Jenbacher units at Frontier: 197 prime + 13 backup = 700MW) are the workhorse: factory-built, deliverable in months, efficient at partial load, and dispatchable 24/7
'Prime' engines run continuously as the main power source; 'backup' units cover maintenance and failures — the same N+1 redundancy logic as data-hall UPS systems, applied to a power plant
Off-grid vs bridge: some deployments are permanent (Frontier runs fully off-grid), others bridge the years until a grid connection matures, then flip to grid-primary with the engines as backup

The ratepayer politics: when data centers strain a grid, households pay through rates. The counter-model — developer funds its own generation and infrastructure (Vantage's Lighthouse arrangement: 70% of new zero-emission capacity to the campus, 30% to the public; a dedicated utility rate) — is becoming a regulatory expectation

sections.heading: Data-center securitization: how an ABS works
bullets: Securitization pools contractual cash flows — here, lease payments from stabilized, tenant-filled data centers — into a bankruptcy-remote entity that issues rated notes against them; investors get bond-like paper, the developer gets cheap long capital

Why data centers securitize well: take-or-pay leases from investment-grade tenants look like the mortgage and franchise-royalty cash flows ABS markets already price — predictable, contracted, asset-backed

Tranching: Class A (senior) notes get paid first and earn ratings like A-; Class B (subordinate) absorbs losses first and earns BBB-tier ratings with higher yield. Slicing risk this way widens the investor base
A 'tap' reopens an existing series to raise more at current pricing without structuring a new deal; a VFN (variable funding note) is a revolver-like tranche drawn as needed during construction

The refinancing flywheel: build with expensive construction debt → lease up → securitize the stabilized asset at investment-grade pricing → recycle proceeds into the next build. Vantage invented this loop for the sector in 2018 and has run 10+ securitizations since, including the first sterling and first euro data-center ABS

Green designations: notes issued under a green-finance framework with a second-party opinion (e.g. Sustainalytics) can tap dedicated ESG capital pools — meaningful when the collateral is energy infrastructure

sections.heading: The private developer's capital stack
bullets: Equity comes from infrastructure investors — asset managers (DigitalBridge), private equity (Silver Lake) and sovereign-wealth/pension funds (GIC, ADIA, AustralianSuper, PSP) — often ring-fenced by region so each investor group funds the geography it underwrote

Construction debt: green loans and borrowing-base facilities fund the build; a construction loan that achieves private investment-grade ratings (like Vantage's $2.25B New Albany loan) prices meaningfully tighter because the pre-leases de-risk it

Giga-projects outgrow any single instrument: the ~$38B JPMorgan/MUFG package for Frontier and Lighthouse (~4-year, ~250bps over benchmark) shows banks syndicating AI campuses like LNG terminals — project-scale infrastructure credit

The exit question for a private platform: hold and refinance forever, sell to a bigger owner, or IPO — a listing prices the whole machine (land bank, leases, development pipeline, financing franchise) in public markets, and reported exploration at a ~$100B mark shows how far the asset class has re-rated

sections.heading: The competitive map: where Vantage sits
bullets: Wholesale/build-to-suit pure-plays: Vantage, Aligned (Tier-II US metros, ODATA in LatAm), STACK (also DigitalBridge-family), CloudHQ, QTS (Blackstone; the largest US land bank), Yondr (absorbed partly into Vantage APAC) — all compete on time-to-power and delivery credibility

Retail/interconnection incumbents: Equinix and Digital Realty are public REITs whose premium is network density and enterprise ecosystems; they build hyperscale through JVs (xScale, etc.) rather than pure landlord bets
Switch: high-density US wholesale with a design-patent identity, taken private by DigitalBridge — a sibling more than a rival

AI-era entrants from the energy side: Crusoe (owns its generation), miner-pivots (Applied Digital, TeraWulf, Core Scientific) converting power positions into leases — competing for the same hyperscaler leases with cheaper power but shorter delivery track records
Vantage's distinctive combination: giga-scale delivery on three continents + the deepest securitization franchise + named Stargate landlord — few peers hold all three at once

sections.heading: The community and regulatory layer
bullets: TIF (tax incremental financing): a locality fronts infrastructure or rebates taxes against the future property-tax uplift a project creates — standard for mega-projects, increasingly contested for data centers

The backlash toolkit is maturing: Port Washington's April 2026 referendum — the first in the US — requires voter approval for TIF packages over $10M for future projects; expect copies wherever giga-campuses land
Water is the sharpest local issue: closed-loop/waterless cooling designs and 'water positive' commitments (restoring more than consumed) exist largely to survive permitting and public hearings

Utility-rate politics: who pays for grid upgrades — the developer or all ratepayers — is becoming the make-or-break question; pledges to 'pay our own way' and dedicated rate structures are the industry's pre-emptive answer

flashcards.q: Wholesale vs retail colocation — what's the difference?
flashcards.a: Retail rents racks/cages to many small customers with interconnection fees; wholesale leases whole halls, buildings or campuses to a few giant tenants on long take-or-pay contracts. Wholesale wins on scale economics, retail on network ecosystem.

flashcards.q: Powered shell vs turnkey — who installs the cooling and UPS?
flashcards.a: In a powered shell the tenant does: the landlord delivers only the building and utility power. In turnkey the landlord delivers the complete environment — distribution, backup, cooling, operations — and the tenant just installs IT gear.

flashcards.q: What makes a take-or-pay lease securitizable?
flashcards.a: Rent is owed on the reserved megawatts regardless of usage, so the cash flow is contractual and predictable — the same profile as mortgages or franchise royalties, which is exactly what ABS investors price.

flashcards.q: Why is a secured grid connection worth more than the land under a campus?
flashcards.a: Interconnection queues for gigawatt loads run 3-5 years. Land is abundant; approved megawatts with a delivery date are the scarce input that determines when revenue can start.

flashcards.q: Walk the campus development lifecycle in four steps.
flashcards.a: (1) Land/power banking — secure acreage and utility megawatts; (2) interconnection queue — wait for or negotiate grid delivery; (3) entitlement and shell — permits, tax agreements, vertical construction, substation; (4) fit-out and energization — plant commissioning, then the tenant's gear. Rent starts at ready-for-service.

flashcards.q: PUE 1.2 vs 1.5 on a 900MW IT campus — how much overhead power is at stake?
flashcards.a: PUE is facility power ÷ IT power. At 1.5 the overhead is ~450MW; at 1.2 it is ~180MW — about 270MW of continuous load saved, which is why efficiency is a siting and design battle, not a rounding error.

flashcards.q: Why does a closed-loop cooling system make WUE 'virtually zero'?
flashcards.a: The chilled water circulates in a sealed loop and rejects heat through air-cooled chillers instead of evaporating water away. No evaporation means almost no consumption — trading a little electrical efficiency for near-total water independence.

flashcards.q: What is a CDU and why does a 250kW rack need one?
flashcards.a: A coolant distribution unit is the heat exchanger and pumping station that moves facility chilled water into the clean liquid loop feeding direct-to-chip cold plates. Above roughly 100kW per rack, air physically cannot carry the heat — liquid must touch the silicon.

flashcards.q: In a 700MW engine microgrid, what do 'prime' and 'backup' units mean?
flashcards.a: Prime engines run continuously as the main power source; backup units stand ready to cover maintenance and failures. It is N+1 redundancy applied to a power plant — e.g. 197 prime + 13 backup reciprocating gas engines.

flashcards.q: Why would a developer run a campus fully off-grid?
flashcards.a: Behind-the-meter generation skips the interconnection queue entirely — power arrives when the engines do (months), not when the utility upgrades transmission (years). The trade: fuel logistics, emissions permitting and running your own power company.

flashcards.q: How does the data-center ABS refinancing flywheel work?
flashcards.a: Build with construction debt → lease up to stabilization → securitize the leased asset into rated notes at investment-grade pricing → recycle the proceeds into the next build. Each turn lowers the cost of capital and funds more development.

flashcards.q: Class A vs Class B notes in a securitization — who takes the first loss?
flashcards.a: Class B (subordinate) absorbs losses first and earns a higher yield with a lower rating (BBB tier); Class A (senior) is paid first and rates higher (A tier). Tranching lets one lease pool serve investors with different risk appetites.

flashcards.q: What is a 'tap' of an existing ABS, and what is a VFN?
flashcards.a: A tap reopens an already-issued note series to raise additional money at current market pricing without building a new structure. A variable funding note is a revolver-like tranche that can be drawn and repaid as construction needs cash.

flashcards.q: Why do giga-campuses get announced only after a tenant commits?
flashcards.a: At $18M+ per megawatt all-in, a 1.4GW campus is a $25B+ commitment — no developer carries that on spec. The mega-scale announcements are really disclosures that a creditworthy tenant (or its cloud provider) already signed.

flashcards.q: What is TIF and why did it trigger the first anti-data-center referendum?
flashcards.a: Tax incremental financing fronts public infrastructure costs against the future property-tax uplift a project creates. Large TIF packages for data centers concentrated local opposition — leading one host town to require voter approval for future TIFs above $10M.

flashcards.q: What does 'water positive' commit a data-center operator to?
flashcards.a: Restoring more water to local freshwater sources (through funded restoration projects) than the campus consumes — paired with low-WUE cooling, it is the design-plus-offset answer to the sharpest community objection.

flashcards.q: How does a build-to-suit developer differ from an energy-first developer like Crusoe or a miner-pivot?
flashcards.a: Build-to-suit developers start from delivery credibility and standardized designs, then solve power (partnerships, microgrids); energy-first players start from owned generation or grid positions, then build the data-center competence. Both sell the same thing — contracted megawatts — with opposite risk profiles.

flashcards.q: Why ring-fence equity by region (separate NA, EMEA, APAC investor groups)?
flashcards.a: Each investor pool underwrites the market, currency and regulatory risk it chose — a pension fund wanting European infrastructure exposure funds EMEA campuses without taking Texas merchant-power risk. It also lets each platform raise at its own pace.
